title: OWASP's 2026 agentic security report: coding agents are now the fastest-growing attack surface, with prompt injection an architectural flaw
summary: OWASP's GenAI Security Project released v2.01 of its State of Agentic AI Security and Governance, and the 2026 edition shifts from theoretical risk to documented incidents — tracking CVEs, vendor advisories, and breach reports across nearly every category of agentic risk. Coding agents are the standout exposure: 28 of 53 tracked agentic projects are coding agents, and the repositories with the most security advisories are all semi-autonomous coding systems (n8n, Claude Code, AutoGPT, Dify, Roo-Code). The report frames prompt injection as an architectural limitation, not a patchable bug, because LLMs cannot reliably separate trusted instructions from untrusted data in a single token stream — it maps to six of OWASP's ten agentic risk categories. It elevates two practical design heuristics: Simon Willison's 'Lethal Trifecta' (private data + untrusted content + external communication = exfiltration risk) and Meta's 'Agents Rule of Two' (an unsupervised agent should hold at most two of those three). Crucially for engineering leaders, it argues safety and security must converge: the Replit production-data-deletion incident and prompt-injection attacks exploit the same over-broad permission models. Compressed regulatory reporting windows (DORA's 4 hours, NIS2's 24 hours) raise the stakes, while shadow-AI deployments remain undetected in 63% of surveyed organizations.
source: OWASP GenAI Security Project (via Help Net Security)
whyItMatters: Coding agents have become the leading agentic attack surface, so security review of the tools that build your software is now as important as reviewing the software itself.

If prompt injection is architectural rather than patchable, defense must come from constraining agent capabilities and permissions ('Rule of Two', isolation, human approval) — not from waiting for a vendor fix.
The same over-broad permissions that cause accidental damage (e.g. agents deleting production data) are what attackers weaponize, so safety and security teams should govern agent permissions jointly.
Shadow-AI invisibility (undetected in 63% of orgs) plus compressed breach-reporting windows means undiscovered agent deployments are a live compliance and incident-response risk.
recommendedActions: Inventory which coding agents and MCP tools have access to repos, secrets, and production systems, and apply the 'Rule of Two' to any agent acting without human approval.
Default coding agents to least-privilege, sandboxed execution with explicit allow/deny rules and mandatory human gates for destructive or external-communication actions.
Treat agent permission models as a joint safety+security control and add agentic incidents to your DORA/NIS2 reporting playbooks.
Run discovery for shadow-AI agent usage and bring it under governance before expanding autonomous workflows.
risksAndCaveats: The report aggregates public CVEs, advisories, and survey data of varying rigor; advisory counts partly reflect project popularity and scrutiny, not only relative insecurity.
Heuristics like the Lethal Trifecta and Rule of Two are useful design guidance, not formal guarantees; they reduce but do not eliminate exfiltration risk.
Survey figures (e.g. 63% shadow-AI) depend on self-reporting and sample composition and may not generalize across sectors.
